lead: PHP strings hold text from forms, files and databases. Built-in functions measure, cut, replace, split, join, format and escape that text. Regular expressions describe a pattern, and PHP's PCRE functions test or rewrite a string against it. You use them to clean a phone number, check an email or date, and escape output before it reaches the browser. The same ideas appear in every server-side language, but PHP's function names and pattern syntax are what you write in this unit.
prereq: You need: 4.1 for variables and strings, and 4.3 for functions and arrays.

blocks.text: PHP strings are byte sequences. Each function returns a new value; assign it to change the variable.

items: strlen($s) returns the number of bytes. For ASCII text, bytes equal characters.
strpos($h, $n) returns the first position of $n in $h, or false. Position 0 is a real match, so compare with !== false.
substr($s, $start, $len) cuts a piece; str_replace($a, $b, $s) replaces every $a with $b.
strtolower, strtoupper, ucfirst change case; trim($s) removes whitespace at both ends: spaces, tabs, vertical tabs, newlines, carriage returns and NUL bytes.
explode($d, $s) splits a string into an array at delimiter $d; implode($g, $arr) joins array items with glue $g.
sprintf("%.2f", $price) formats a number to two decimals. htmlspecialchars($s, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8') turns &, <, >, " and ' into HTML entities. nl2br($s) inserts <br /> before each newline.

blocks.text: Example: $parts = explode(" ", "98765 43210") gives two items. implode("", $parts) joins them back. For Indian text, bytes differ from characters; use mb_* functions when needed.

PCRE means Perl Compatible Regular Expressions; PHP uses it for pattern matching. A pattern sits between delimiters, usually slashes: /pattern/. preg_match($pat, $s) returns 1 if found, 0 if not, and false on error. It stops at the first match. preg_match_all returns the number of matches. preg_replace($pat, $rep, $s) returns a new string with matches replaced. preg_split($pat, $s) splits by a pattern.

blocks.where: ^ is the start anchor; [6-9] is one digit from 6 to 9; \d is any digit 0–9; {9} repeats exactly nine times; $ is the end anchor.

items: Anchors: ^ start, $ end. Without them, a match inside a longer string also returns 1.
Classes: [6-9] one digit from 6 to 9; \d digit, \w word character (letter, digit, underscore), \s space, tab or newline.
Quantifiers: * zero or more, + one or more, ? zero or one, {9} exactly nine.
Groups (...) and alternation |: /(cat|dog)/ matches either word.
Modifiers after the closing slash: i ignores case, m makes anchors match at line breaks, u treats the string as UTF-8.

blocks.text: Use single-quoted PHP strings for patterns: '/^[6-9]\d{9}$/'. In a double-quoted string PHP interprets escapes such as \n, \t, \\ and \1, so a pattern containing a backslash-digit sequence or a literal backslash can change; single quotes pass the pattern to PCRE unchanged.
Validation checks the shape of user input before it reaches the database or a page. Clean first, then test, then escape when printing.

items: Read the field, for example $phone = $_POST['phone']. Form handling is in 4.5.
Remove spaces with preg_replace('/\s+/', '', $phone); this turns 98765 43210 into 9876543210.
Test the whole string with preg_match('/^[6-9]\d{9}$/', $phone). Use === 1 for valid.
For email, a simple pattern is /^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[a-z]{2,}$/i. It checks one @, no spaces, and a dot in the domain; it does not prove the mailbox exists.
For a date, /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/ checks only the shape YYYY-MM-DD. It accepts 2024-99-99; use checkdate($m, $d, $y) for a real calendar date.
Escape every user string before HTML output: echo htmlspecialchars($name, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8');. This blocks script injection in the page.

blocks.text: Regular expressions match patterns; they are not a full HTML parser. Do not use one regex to read nested tags. Use DOMDocument or an HTML parser for that job.

figure.caption: The space is already gone after preg_replace, so each number is exactly ten digits; the first digit must sit in 6–9, which gives result 1 for 9 and result 0 for 5. The ^ and $ anchors force the pattern to cover the whole string, not part of it.

spec.title: After removing spaces
spec.aria: Two cleaned ten-digit phone numbers tested against ^[6-9]\d{9}$: the first digit 9 is inside 6–9 so preg_match returns 1, while the first digit 5 is outside so it returns 0.

examples.question: A form sends $phone = '98765 43210'. Remove spaces with preg_replace('/\s+/', '', $phone), then test preg_match('/^[6-9]\d{9}$/', $phone). Show the cleaned value and the result for this input and for '5876543210'.
steps: Start with $phone = '98765 43210', length 11 bytes including one space.
preg_replace('/\s+/', '', $phone) matches the space with \s+ and replaces it with an empty string. Cleaned value: 9876543210.
Test 9876543210 against ^[6-9]\d{9}$: first digit 9 is in 6–9, then nine digits follow, and $ is reached. Result: 1.
Start with '5876543210'. There is no space, so the cleaned value is 5876543210.
Test 5876543210: first digit 5 is not in [6-9], so the anchored pattern fails. Result: 0.
examples.answer: The cleaned value for the first input is 9876543210, so preg_match returns 1 and the number is valid. The second number starts with 5, so the result is 0 and it is invalid.
examples.check:
import re
phone = '98765 43210'
clean = re.sub(r'\s+', '', phone)
print(int(clean))
print(1 if re.match(r'^[6-9]\d{9}$', clean) else 0)
phone2 = '5876543210'
clean2 = re.sub(r'\s+', '', phone2)
print(1 if re.match(r'^[6-9]\d{9}$', clean2) else 0)

code.code:
<?php
$phone = '98765 43210';
$clean = preg_replace('/\s+/', '', $phone);
$first = preg_match('/^[6-9]\d{9}$/', $clean);
echo $clean . "\n";
echo $first . "\n";
$phone2 = '5876543210';
$clean2 = preg_replace('/\s+/', '', $phone2);
$second = preg_match('/^[6-9]\d{9}$/', $clean2);
echo $second . "\n";
?>

traps: Missing delimiters: preg_match('^[6-9]\d{9}$', $s) is an error; use /.../ or #...#.
Unanchored pattern: /[6-9]\d{9}/ matches inside an 11-digit number; add ^ and $.
strpos returns 0 for a match at the start; 0 == false is true, so test with === false.
A backslash in a double-quoted PHP string is an escape; write patterns in single quotes, or double the backslashes.
A date regex checks shape only; it accepts impossible dates such as 2024-02-31.

quiz.a: 1 for a match, 0 for no match, and false on error.

quiz.q: Why escape output with htmlspecialchars before printing user text into HTML?
quiz.a: User text may contain <, >, & or quotes. The function turns them into entities, so the browser shows text instead of running code. This helps prevent cross-site scripting.

quiz.q: Write a full anchored pattern for a 10-digit Indian mobile number whose first digit is 6–9.
quiz.a: /^[6-9]\d{9}$/. The first digit is 6–9, and \d{9} adds the other nine digits.
987654. Each run of spaces is replaced by an empty string.

quiz.q: Why is if (strpos($s, 'a')) wrong for checking whether 'a' exists?
quiz.a: strpos returns 0 when 'a' is at the start. In PHP, 0 is false in a condition, so a real match is missed. Compare with !== false.

quiz.q: The date pattern /^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$/ accepts 2024-99-99. What does this show?
quiz.a: The regex checks the shape only: four digits, dash, two digits, dash, two digits. It does not check month or day ranges. Use checkdate for a real calendar date.

quiz.q: Give a simple email pattern and state one limitation.
quiz.a: /^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[a-z]{2,}$/i checks one @, no spaces, and a dot in the domain. It does not prove the mailbox exists and may accept some invalid addresses.

quiz.q: What does the u modifier do in a PCRE pattern?
quiz.a: It treats the subject and pattern as UTF-8, so characters such as é or Devanagari letters are handled as characters, not bytes.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production PHP uses PCRE features such as named groups, lookahead and Unicode properties. Regex engines can suffer ReDoS when nested quantifiers backtrack badly. For HTML and JSON, use parsers and encoders, not regex. Search for PCRE2, ReDoS, named capture groups and PHP filter_var.
